newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FEATURE - Bulgaria's Gypsies see no way out of misery.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bulgaria's Gypsies see no way out of misery.

text.p: Economic crisis will bring hardship to homes throughout Bulgaria this winter but the 2,000 destitute and despised Gypsies in the Maglizh ghetto are at the bottom of the social heap.
Ragged and often barefoot, families are crammed 10 to a room in dilapidated shacks without water or electricity.

"We can only see as far as surviving this winter, but even that seems very difficult now," said Petar Kolev, who has lived all his 30 years in Maglizh, 180 km (112 miles) southeast of the capital, Sofia.
"Without work, relying only on social welfare which has not been paid for months, we are starving to death."
The country's 300,000 Gypsies have traditionally aroused contempt and suspicion among Bulgarians. Uneducated and unemployed, they see a bleak future.
They are thought to have first come to Europe from the Punjab region of India around the 10th century.

In the 19th century they were mainly craftsmen -- basketmakers, combmakers, blacksmiths and tinkers -- but the emergence of manufacturing industry at the turn of the century limited the scope of their activities.

They were nomadic until the 1960s, when the communist government began a campaign of assimilation, severely curbing their religious and cultural traditions and forcing them to settle in Soviet-style collective farms or in housing projects.
After the collapse of communism in 1989 they lost access to jobs previously reserved for them and many of their welfare benefits.
More then 70 percent are believed to be jobless and the same number are thought to be illiterate. Many resort to theft, prostitution, gambling and begging.
"How can we make a living when we are unwanted even for the dirtiest jobs?" asked Nikola Dobrev, a young man in Maglizh.
Soaring prices mean small jobs like gathering herbs for sale no longer raise enough money to feed large families.
Maria Simeonova, mother of three children, said she had to steal bread from a bakery last week. "If you had children who hadn't eaten for days, you'd steal too, I'm sure," she said.
Eleonora Kaneva, a Bulgarian doctor who has worked with Gypsies for 18 years in the Filipovtsi ghetto, on the outskirts of Sofia, said not only the state was at fault.

"It is true that there is huge unemployment among Gypsies and they are not wanted for any jobs," she said. "But it is also true that they are not the most reliable workers. Sometimes, when hired, they do not turn up at work for days."
Kaneva said that during communist rule many Gypsy families were given state housing, but sold their apartments and returned to the ghettos.

Human rights groups like Amnesty International have documented many cases of police beatings and other ill-treatment of Gypsies and criticised the government for doing nothing to protect the Roma community.
A report by the U.S. State Department in March 1996 accused Bulgaria of "degrading treatment" of Gypsies.

Residents told a visiting reporter that police had surrounded the area two days earlier and beaten anyone who was outside, including elderly people and children, accusing them of stealing from the town.

"It is not an excuse, but due to the lack of jobs many Gypsies have turned to crime," said Petar Georgiev, the only Roma deputy in the Bulgarian parliament, who was elected on the ticket of the ruling Bulgarian Socialist Party.

Georgiev, who said he had never been to the Maglizh ghetto, said the government was considering a programme to offer Gypsies jobs in cities or on the land to try to secure at least one working person per family.
But it is not a high priority for a government struggling to make ends meet through the winter and avoid default on its foreign debt. "It seems they are going to starve this winter," Georgiev said.
But the Gypsies of Maglizh cannot share most Bulgarians' hope that proposals to halt the collapse of the lev currency will bring some relief next spring.
"My parents have spent all their lives here in misery, and so will my children," said mother of six, Nedyalka Hristova. "There is no way out for us from this plight."
